rulings.text: Verify the page budget; a second page with a few dangling lines is a major or blocker.
A one-page resume must never go over one page.
Rendered PDF must be one page with balanced margins and a prominent header.
A no page limit setting does not override industry norms; three or more pages is a major outside academic roles.
Under four years of paid software work, a second page is a major.
Under four to five years, the one-page ceiling is hard; five or more years may use two pages only if page 1 stands alone and page 2 is at least 40 percent full of high-signal content.
A second page under about 40 percent full reads as failed compression and is a major.
A second page 40 to 55 percent full on an eligible 5+ year profile is a nit; never force-fill it.
A second page at least 60 percent full on an eligible 5+ year profile is fine.
Check the built page for orphan one- or two-word line wraps.
No bullet may end on an orphan of one or two words.
No orphan one- or two-word wraps.
No bullet or skills line may end on a one- or two-word orphan line.
No bullet or skills line ends in a one- or two-word orphan.
A named project entry should carry a clickable link to its repo, PR or write-up.
Every project should link to its public repo, PR or issue.
Check embedded link annotations; projects making high-scrutiny claims should be clickable.
Link the top projects first; flagship entries without links block quick verification.
Deep technical claims are more credible with a direct link to the commits or issue reports.
Add working links for every project, paper and PR to raise verifiable proof.
A link deliberately withheld until a repo is public is a nit; attach it once published.
Link a project once its code is public; the missing link is a nit.
A link withheld until a repo is public is a nit.
Attach public links to flagship repos and papers on the sheet.
A withheld link for an unpublished repo is only a nit.
Link when public; until then a nit.
Count and verify embedded clickable links in the built PDF.
An unpublished repo link is no reason to hold a ready sheet; attach it later.
A pending link for an unpublished repo is a nit.
Do not block submission on an unpublished repo link.
Header contact links must work and be embedded.
Every flagship paper, repo and external PR needs a working embedded link.
Link the specific proof item, not a profile page.
A link deliberately withheld until publication is a single nit, not a failure.
Extracted link annotations show working links on header contacts and all public repos, papers and PRs.
A long stretch without paid software work after an unrelated program draws scrutiny of the timeline.
Unexplained multi-year gaps are flagged fast, so recent dated work should cover the span; research bullets are judged on methodology.
A multi-year stretch with no paid software work draws skepticism unless dated technical activity is visible across it.
A long stretch between paid roles stays a nit when dated volunteer work and study partly cover it.
Fill multi-year visual gaps with dated, verifiable work so the timeline has no empty stretch on a quick scan.
An empty gap between study and recent work is rejected before projects are read; fill it with verified dated entries such as volunteer work, hackathons, research and merged open-source PRs.
Measure blank time across all dated sections, not only between paid roles, and judge trailing gaps more strictly.
No gap penalty inside an active degree window.
Zero to three blank months after graduation is normal and never flagged.
Four to six blank months is a nit for early-career and nothing at mid-level.
Seven to twelve blank months is a major; a historical 7-9 month gap followed by continuous work drops to a nit.
Over twelve blank months, or over nine trailing to the present, is a blocker.
A long gap between paid roles on an early-career resume is a nit when dated research, projects or open source bridge it.
Compute the longest interval with no dated entry in any section, apply thresholds to it, then check paid-role gaps for mid-level targets.
A multi-year visual gap causes drop-off; fill gaps with verified engineering work such as volunteer work, hackathon wins, research and merged PRs.
No unexplained multi-month or multi-year blank gaps in recent history.
A short or fixed-scope engagement must be labeled as a contract (or volunteer role) so it does not read like a failed full-time job.
A very short recent role with thin output reads like a failed probation unless it is labeled as a scoped contract.
Label short contracts and unpaid roles; never present them as continuous full-time employment.
Experience must be reverse-chronological by start date.
Experience is strictly newest start first.
Sections other than Experience default to newest first; relevance may override that per posting.
A language listed in the skills section must be backed by real work visible on the page; one with no supporting bullet is flagged.
Remove any skill, language or practice that no shipped bullet supports, and align the skills list to what you can defend in an interview.
Every skill in the skills section needs at least one bullet backing it.
Reviewers check every listed skill against the bullets; orphaned skills read as stale keyword stuffing or unverified claims.
When a bullet is deleted, drop any skill whose only backing bullet it was.
Sub-skills named in parentheses need to appear in a bullet, or come off the skills line.
After each edit, audit the skills section against the bullets that remain on that sheet.
A skill whose only bullet was removed becomes an orphan and must come off.
Close an orphaned skill by adding a bullet that exercises it or removing the skill.
Remove a practice from the skills section when no bullet backs it.
A practice in the skills line with no mention in any bullet should be dropped or tied to a bullet.
When adding a project back, also update the skills line for the languages it brings.
Every listed skill must trace to a concrete bullet.
Do not add a language to the skills line without production bullets behind it.
Every item in the skills section must be backed by at least one bullet.
After deleting a bullet, drop any skill whose only backing it was.
Every skills and subtitle token is proven in at least one bullet.
A language named in an entry heading is listed on the Languages line.
Use one form for approximate values: a plain tilde, not math sim symbols mixed with the word about.
Use a single plain tilde for approximations throughout.
Contact details must survive plain-text extraction: write out the profile URLs rather than relying on icons alone.
Contact icons must be paired with written-out URLs so plain-text extraction keeps them.
Extracted text must read in a single column in order.
Extracted text needs clean punctuation, no broken ligatures, garbled glyphs, tables or text boxes.
Use standard section headings that ATS parsers segment cleanly.
Never shrink body fonts or collapse the header to fit more lines.
Do not open bullets with casual verbs like Got; use concrete engineering verbs.
Replace weak openers like Took, Got, Matched and Ran with outcome verbs.
Lead with a strong active engineering verb and avoid filler openers and passive duties.
Casual openers like Hit weaken a bullet.
Weak verbs and symptom-first framing fail the outcome slot; a count of attempts is not an outcome.
Passive weak openers hide the functional outcome.
Passive openers and leading with raw activity fail the outcome slot.
Replace weak verbs; a shared-credit verb is acceptable only when truthful attribution needs it.
Every bullet starts with a concrete outcome verb.
Line counts on a project and agent-authorship phrasing make a resume read as bloated; leaving them off is cleaner.
Line-of-code bragging on projects and unbacked skill keywords are standard rejection triggers.
Presenting agent-built work through test counts and harness mechanics invites AI-slop skepticism; show engineering judgment instead.
Large line counts and test counts on an agent-assisted project signal bloat rather than engineering strength.
Test and mutant counts on a small utility read as inflation.
Synthetic-sounding mutation and unit-test counts should come off the page.
A clause like merged via code review and a CI gate describes merge hygiene, not an outcome.
Frame CI as ownership of the gate you set up, not as a merge-review checklist.
Trailing clauses such as passed review or built from a reviewed design doc read like process notes, not outcomes.

params.note: later called a gray zone when it backs a posting keyword

rulings.text: State ownership of the CI setup rather than reporting that a PR passed review.
Raw line counts and test counts on an agent-assisted repo read as vanity metrics; name a concrete engineering property instead.
A line count on an open external PR and a test count behind strong operational metrics were judged harmless.
Drop line counts from unmerged pull requests; say what the fix does.
All controllable vanity counts should be off the page before submission.
Showing line and test counts for a shipped project was judged acceptable.
A bullet carrying line and test counts for a co-built project was judged resolved.
Remove size and test counts from co-built repos as an AI-slop flag.
Line counts on an open PR and test counts behind strong metrics were judged non-blocking.
Remove unit-test counts and unmerged-PR line counts while keeping keyword coverage.
A list of CI tools is not a measure of result.
Report volume and test counts as scale evidence.
Showing project size and counts as scale evidence was recommended.
Do not show line counts for personal or agent-assisted projects.
Do not show line counts on unmerged pull requests; say what the fix does.
Do not show raw unit-test or mutation-test counts.
Do not add trailing clauses about review and merge hygiene.
Frame CI as ownership of the gate you set up, and only when it backs a listed skill.
Remove line and test counts on an agent-co-built app.
Remove test counts that sit beside stronger cost and cap proof.
Remove line counts on an open PR.
Remove CI-verified checklist clauses.
No repo line counts, unmerged-PR line counts, raw test or mutant counts, or merge-checklist buzzwords.
Do not copy a posting's keywords into the skills section when nothing on the page backs them; reviewers spot this at once.
Technologies actually used in bullets belong in the skills section too, including the named ML framework.
Add keywords the bullets already back (retrieval, embeddings, vector search) to the skills section; missing them costs free ATS matches.
Add technologies a bullet exercises, such as retrieval and vector-search tools, to the skills section for keyword coverage.
Add exercised technologies to the skills section as ATS keywords.
Posting phrases like A or B and example lists are alternatives; satisfying one covers the others.
An OR-group or example list already met by one backed member carries no severity for the others.
A standalone required language with strong recent evidence that is left off the page is a major to fix by adding a backing bullet.
Treat A-or-B and one-or-more lists as OR-groups and charge nothing for siblings once one member is backed.
Keep every required posting keyword when cutting for space.
High-signal technologies practiced in bullets appear in the skills section; duplicate wrapping terms are trimmed.
Promote keywords that bullets exercise into the skills section.
For ML roles, name the framework, data scale, training or serving setup and evaluation used, not only the headline result.
Do not cut the strongest production-work bullets from a sheet when they exist on a sibling version; restore them.
Do not strip the strongest comparative result and method detail from a research entry; name framework, data and compute scale.
When a bullet loses its outcome, add a verifiable scope detail such as team size or delivery target.
A research or ML result should list corpus scale and training stack next to the headline result.
State dataset size, compute and your own contribution inside a team-trained result.
A pipeline-fix bullet should state the scale it protected.
Anchor pipeline work to the volume it served.
When two bullets cover one effort, merge them so the verified measure covers both.
A bare Fixed with no scale reads like a single small ticket; add the verified scale.
A bullet that stops at diagnosis without saying what landed or changed lacks an outcome.
A debugging bullet that stops at diagnosis must say what fix or outcome landed.
A mechanism clause must name what was actually done or tested, not a vague phrase.
A bullet that diagnoses a problem should also report the fix and the result after it.
A bullet that describes a feature instead of an accomplishment fails the outcome slot.
Meeting a baseline duty is not an accomplishment; show proactive engineering and its scale.
A bullet without a measure passes only if it is a sharp outcome plus mechanism that names a real engineering property, and the page elsewhere carries strong numbers.
A speedup or score is weak evidence if its sample is tiny or it drops quality unmeasured; report the quality measure alongside it on a meaningful eval set.
A safety or guardrail claim should carry evaluation numbers (test-suite size, block rate, false-positive rate), not just a description of the guards.
A tiny sample and a speedup from switching a setting off need accuracy or quality reported with them to count as evidence.
Do not advertise a tiny test set as proof of quality parity; drop the parenthetical or back it with a real benchmark.
A latency win from turning off a feature needs an accompanying quality measure to be meaningful.
For ML roles, evaluation rigor matters; a very small test set presented as proof signals toy-scale evaluation.
Safety work claims need red-team size, attack-success change and false-refusal numbers to read as systematic.
Safety claims relying only on prompt text need evaluation counts and code-level checks to be credible.
A latency claim without a quality or regression measure is only half a measurement.
Write each bullet as an accomplishment, the measure of it, then the action that delivered it, in that order.
The measure must show how big or well verified the outcome was, not a bare activity count.
Join the mechanism to the outcome with by, not with.
Lead with the outcome, not the activity or its cost.
Lead with the user outcome so outcome, measure and mechanism read in order.
Use the accomplishment, measure, action formula for bullets.
A flagship claim needs a measure; opaque units and activity counts unrelated to value fail it.
Connect the mechanism to the outcome with by, not with.
A raw volume count that is trivially produced by the hardware inflates the claim; cut it.
Do not force a numeric measure onto a bullet; a clean outcome plus mechanism bullet passes when the rest of the page has real numbers.
Add a measure to such a bullet only when real user or runtime data exists.
A hardware measurement count that reflects real test volume, not code size, is a defensible gray-zone item.
An outcome-plus-mechanism bullet without a number beats a forced measure, when stronger numbers elsewhere anchor the page.
Add a measure only with real runtime or adoption data.
Authorship-scoping and design-doc clauses may stay on a track when they keep authorship truthful or back required keywords.
When a bullet has no honest outcome measure, leave the measure off rather than inventing a vanity one.
Add a measure back only when real external metrics exist.
Separate real slop counts from defensible gray-zone items before cutting signal.
Keep specific failure evidence that proves root-cause isolation.
An iteration count may stay only when immediately followed by the concrete fixes.
A hardware sweep volume is a gray-zone item; optional to trim.
An authorship-scoping clause stays when it keeps credit honest.
A design-doc clause is acceptable only when it deliberately backs a required keyword on that track.
No vanity measure is invented to fill the slot.
On a role-specific sheet, projects unrelated to the posting's domain should not dominate the section, especially unlinked ones.
On a GenAI posting, lead Projects with LLM evals, guardrails, embeddings and retrieval before unrelated systems work.
Order projects by relevance to the posting; the most relevant work goes first.
Project order should put the posting's core themes first so a recruiter sees them first.
Lead Projects with the entries most relevant to the posting.
Order projects by relevance to the posting, not by date.
For LLM roles, lead with eval, guardrail and retrieval projects, ahead of unrelated systems work.
For systems and early-career roles, lead with deep low-level debugging work.
Projects are ordered by relevance to the posting.
A language named only in a project subtitle, with no bullet showing work in it, counts as unbacked.
A language in a project tag and a practice in the skills line must each be backed by a bullet or removed.
A language left in a project tag with no bullet behind it looks like a leftover from another draft.
Project tech tags must be backed by a bullet too.
Phrase bullets in precise engineering terms, not conversational wording.
Express costs and savings in portable units (dollars, tokens, percentages) rather than vendor-specific counters.
Replace casual phrasing with precise production-monitoring terms.
Do not use opaque platform counters; give dollars, tokens or time.
Cost figures need a baseline in dollars, tokens or percent.
Avoid first-person casual phrasing in impact bullets; use formal engineering wording.
Normalize costs to dollars, tokens or time.
Do not compress concrete root causes into a bare count; the specific causes are what make the bullet stand out.
Say what an open pull request does and in which language so a screener sees it at once.
Replace raw constants and flags with plain engineering terms, and fix domain typos that change the meaning.
A bare bug count should name two or three of the actual fixes.
Remove raw flag names and fix typos that change meaning.
Name the specific fixes behind a bug count.
Name the concrete engineering pieces behind a vague specs and gates clause.

rulings.text: Swap vague run counts and vendor units for portable metrics such as test counts, dollars and token caps.
Name the exact metric (for example sales lift) instead of a vague word like gain.
A bare bug count hides the real engineering; name the causes.
Do not compress concrete root causes into a count.
Replace raw flags and internal names with plain engineering concepts.
Fix domain-specific typos that change meaning.
Do not use undefined tool-specific vocabulary.
No opaque insider names, raw flags or domain typos.
A project entry must hold only bullets that belong under its heading; unrelated work needs its own heading.
A standalone tool bullet under an unrelated project title mixes projects; split them or use an accurate umbrella heading.
When two related bullets share an entry, give the entry an umbrella heading that covers both.
Rename a project entry to an umbrella heading when its bullets cover related but distinct work.
Use an accurate umbrella heading for combined bullets and keep the concrete cause details.
A bullet under a heading about a different topic needs an umbrella heading or its own entry.
Do not put an unrelated bullet under a narrow project title; split the entry or use an accurate umbrella heading.
The strongest content must be on page 1, since humans decide there.
Strip authorship and size phrasing that undersells or pads the work; state architecture and concrete bugs caught instead.
A clause that scopes authorship truthfully may stay even if it reads slightly formal.
The mechanism clause must name every real cause so the result is not credited to one change alone.
In team work, the mechanism clause should name your own contribution, not a team verb.
Never stretch paid tenure beyond real dates.
Never present roadmap ideas or unbuilt features as shipped work.
When agents wrote much of the code or the work was a team effort, scope authorship truthfully rather than claiming sole credit.
Separate resume defects, fixable by editing, from role-fit gaps that editing cannot fix.
Diagnose tenure shortfalls honestly, never suggest stretching dates, and say when an otherwise clean higher-level sheet is still worth sending to win down-level or external routing.
For mid-level targets, a long paid-role gap bridged only by personal projects is a role-fit warning.
Total contiguous paid tenure against the target band is a structural limit that editing cannot fix.
Bullets should describe engineering work and its results, not meeting rituals, pull-request counts or non-code admin tasks.
Replace process claims and non-code admin items with the actual engineering shipped: code, interfaces, failure handling, tests.
A bullet about non-code escalation wastes space in a software role; replace it with engineering contribution.
Listing personal scripts and self-directed work as a job in Experience reads as gap-filling and crowds out real paid work.
Move self-directed work out of Experience into Projects, keeping only items that are public and verifiable, with live links.
A multi-year self-directed entry in Experience built from personal scripts looks like gap padding.
A time-saved figure that is implausible on its face damages trust in every other number; use a figure you can defend strictly.
One implausible number makes the reader discount every other metric on the page.
A large time-saved figure invites probing; be ready to say whether it was active effort or elapsed wall-clock time.
Reframe time-saved claims around active effort removed or delivery time cut, so they survive probing.
Do not hedge a truthful strong number to prepare for deep interviews; restore punchy, truthful metrics.

params.reverses: earlier advice to make claims more conservative

rulings.text: Do not hedge or dull strong, factual numbers because an interviewer might probe them later; prepare the defense after the invite.
Keep a truthful phrase punchy if it wins the scan and can be honestly defended.
Never put fabricated figures, broken projects or zero-code repositories on any sheet.
A broken prototype must not take page space that shipped recent work needs.
A very old hackathon with no surviving code or detail is not evidence for a skill.
Using a runtime or writing style docs in a language is not engineering in that language.
With only weak evidence, make no resume edit; report a role-fit warning instead.
Route a missing skill backed only by invalid evidence to a separate role-fit warning, never a resume-edit severity, so nobody stuffs broken or stale projects.
Leave out broken prototypes, empty or doc-only repos and projects whose claims fail inspection.
